the presence of other people reduces the probability that a bystander will help a victim, and the magnitude of this effect increases with the number of bystanders and the size of the emergency.

1) the presence of other people reduces bystanders' willingness to intervene in an emergency; and 2) bystanders' willingness is reduced to the extent that they perceive the others as also being aware of the emergency.
bystanders are more likely to help when they are the only ones present, and when they perceive the situation to be an emergency.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the presence of other observers, and their apparent willingness to help, decreases a person's willingness to help.
we found that people were less likely to help when other people were around than when they were alone, that people are more likely to help when they are in a group than when they are alone.
